Talk/Poster Title: GLACIER: A Multimodal Student-Teacher Foundation Model for Molecular Property Prediction
Author(s): Emily Nguyen, Yongchan Hong, Harsh Toshniwal, Yan Liu, Andreas Luttens
Abstract: Deep learning models facilitate the discovery of molecules with tailored properties among billions of candidate compounds. However, the computational burden to develop and deploy state-of-the-art models continuously increases, limiting their scalability. Most large-scale models are unimodal in nature and overlook the potential to leverage complementary molecular data modalities. To address these shortcomings, this paper introduces the Graph-Language Alignment for Chemical Inference and Exploration using Representations (GLACIER) model, a student-teacher framework that integrates molecular graphs, SMILES strings, and physicochemical descriptors to learn rich molecular embeddings. Our framework consists of three stages: (1) we pretrain three student encoders on 100,000 drug-like molecules: a message-passing neural network for molecular graphs, a transformer-based encoder for SMILES strings, and a multilayer perceptron for physicochemical descriptors, (2) we fuse these student modalities using a novel Finsler geometry-aware module, and (3) distill complementary knowledge from large teacher models, including MiniMol and MolFormer, into a single lightweight model via contrastive learning. We demonstrate that GLACIER is a robust framework that delivers high predictive performance and computational efficiency in complex molecular property prediction tasks. Our code is publicly available at this URL: https://github.com/eemokey/glacier.

Talk/Poster Title: Intracranial Internal Carotid Artery Calcification Shifts Toward Higher Attenuation With Age
Author(s): Fangyun (Cecilia) Liu, Helena C. Chui, Margaret Gatz, Wendy J. Mack, Hillard Kaplan, Andrei Irimia
Abstract:
Background: Intracranial internal carotid artery calcification (iICAC) is commonly summarized using a single attenuation threshold. However, CT attenuation may reflect the degree of mineralization, so attenuation-specific measures may capture biological variation that total volume cannot resolve. We examined age-related differences in iICAC attenuation and whether these patterns were preserved within the C4-C5 bend, a region of pronounced curvature associated with complex hemodynamics and arterial wall stress.
Methods: Noncontrast brain CT scans from 1,232 Tsimane and Moseten adults aged 40 years and older were analyzed. The intracranial internal carotid arteries were manually delineated, and iICAC volume was classified as low attenuation (60-89 HU), intermediate attenuation (90-129 HU), or high attenuation (130-500 HU). An automated pipeline isolated the C4-C5 bend using the most anterior arterial point, a ±5-slice window, and a fixed spatial constraint. Calcification burden was compared across age groups in the whole artery and C4-C5 bend.
Results: Attenuation-specific calcification changed systematically with age. Low- and intermediate-attenuation components showed modest positive age-group gradients and tended to plateau in older groups, whereas high-attenuation calcification remained low at younger ages and was dramatically higher after age 60. Its contribution to total burden therefore increased progressively with age, while the low-attenuation proportion remained relatively stable. The C4-C5 bend contained approximately 40%-50% of total iICAC and preserved the whole-artery attenuation pattern. Within the bend, the total calcified proportion increased from approximately 25% in the youngest group to 50% in the oldest group, driven primarily by high-attenuation calcification.
Conclusions: Aging was associated not only with greater iICAC burden but also with a shift toward higher-attenuation mineralization. Attenuation stratification therefore provides biological information about calcification composition beyond total volume alone. The preservation of these patterns in the C4-C5 bend supports its value as a focused regional measure for studying intracranial vascular aging.

Talk/Poster Title: Metabolic Reprogramming and Therapeutic Vulnerabilities in the Tumor Microenvironment Revealed by Multi-scale Network Geometry
Author(s): Handan Cetin, Paul Bogdan, Shannon M Mumenthaler, Stacey D Finley
Abstract: The tumor microenvironment comprises diverse cell populations that coordinate metabolic activities to sustain malignant growth, yet the systems-level organization of these interactions remains poorly understood. Here, we present an integrated framework combining single-cell transcriptomics, genome-scale metabolic modeling, and multi-scale network geometry to decode metabolic coordination in colorectal cancer. We demonstrate that FAP+ cancer-associated fibroblasts and MARCO+ tumor-associated macrophages undergo extensive reprogramming, establishing metabolic division of labor: fibroblasts specialize in amino acid and fatty acid metabolism while macrophages adopt cancer-like nucleotide biosynthesis programs. Systematic knockout analysis identified 19 tumor-selective vulnerabilities in branched-chain amino acid catabolism, with MAOB validated as a prognostic marker through patient survival analysis. To reveal architectural organization, we applied multifractal geometric characterization and Ollivier-Ricci curvature analysis for the first time to flux-weighted metabolic networks derived from context-specific genome-scale models. While conventional network metrics failed to distinguish tumors from normal phenotypes, multifractal analysis successfully separated tissue states through coordinated architectural changes across hierarchical scales. Role transition analysis revealed that 20--25% of metabolites undergo functional reorganization, with prostaglandin and bile acid derivatives emerging as critical communication hubs between stromal populations. Curvature analysis identified pathway-specific geometric remodeling in fatty acid metabolism (fibroblasts) and leukotriene metabolism (macrophages). Our findings establish that metabolic adaptation represents ecosystem-level network reorganization rather than isolated pathway changes, providing a generalizable framework for identifying therapeutic strategies targeting cooperative metabolic networks.

Talk/Poster Title: Trustworthy Protein-Ligand Binding Affinity Prediction via Reliability-Aware Multi-Engine Fusion
Author(s): Yongchan Hong, Defu Cao, Wenjin Liu, Thomas Ku, Jordy Homing Lam, Emily Nguyen, Willie Neiswanger, Vsevolod Katritch, Yan Liu
Abstract: Accurate protein-ligand binding affinity prediction is central to computational drug discovery, yet modern docking engines frequently disagree without indicating which prediction to trust. Consensus scoring and ensemble methods improve mean accuracy but treat all predictions identically without interpretable confidence measures or uncertainty decomposition, ignoring the chemical context of each protein-ligand pair. To address this limitation, we introduce RELIABLE-BA (RELIABiLity-aware Evidential fusion for Binding Affinity), an evidential framework for multi-engine binding affinity prediction. Our model comprises three steps: (1) modeling each engine as an evidential expert via Normal-Inverse-Gamma distributions, (2) scaling epistemic uncertainty through learned reliability from molecular context while preserving each expert's predictive mean, and (3) fusing experts through closed-form aggregation that captures both individual uncertainty and inter-engine disagreement. Experiments on the PDBBind and BDB2020+ benchmarks demonstrate competitive point prediction with substantially improved uncertainty calibration, and additional validation on the SARS-CoV-2 Mpro dataset and 5HT2A receptor demonstrates applicability to clinically relevant drug targets. Crucially, these uncertainty estimates enable reliable filtering of protein-ligand pairs, reducing prediction error by up to ~25% when retaining only high-confidence pairs. To our knowledge, RELIABLE-BA is the first multi-engine binding affinity prediction framework to combine evidential fusion with context-dependent reliability, offering a principled path toward trustworthy AI-guided drug discovery. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/yongchand/RELIABLE-BA.

Talk/Poster Title: FastSD: A Wraparound Sparse Dynamic Programming Approach to String Decomposition
Author(s): Ishaan Thota and Mark Chaisson
Abstract:
Centromeric DNA has long been among the most challenging regions of the genome to analyze. Despite the sequence of these regions being important to mitosis and meiosis,  they tend to be highly repetitive and mutate rapidly, making de novo assembly and sequence level analyses difficult. Recent developments in long-read sequencing data and assembly algorithms fully resolve these centromeric sequences, but analysis of variation remains a difficult hurdle. The complexity of centromeric variation may be simplified by first annotating the repeat decomposition: the order and segmentation of motif sequences that form a centromeric sequence with respect to a canonical motif library. The fidelity of the repeat decomposition to the original sequence is governed by the size of the motif library. We first present a clustering approach to define representative motif sets of increasing resolution from 200 to 2,000 motifs that may be used to annotate the motif decomposition of additional centromeres.  While original methods such as StringDecomposer were written to find decomposition using libraries with fewer than 100 motifs, the runtime scales by the total size of the library and centromeric sequence, leading to prohibitive runtimes for large motif libraries.
 
 To address this, we developed FastSD, a decomposition approach using sparse wraparound dynamic programming to perform rapid centromeric repeat decomposition at scale. It approximates the exact result by identifying exact k-mer matches between the target sequence and chaining them together to find a maximal scoring path, then converting it to a sequence of motifs. The runtime of FastSD scales with the number of k-mer matches, running up to 736 times faster than comparable tools on the same input, while maintaining accuracy that comparable to tools solving for the exact centromeric decomposition problem. We used FastSD to annotate 65 centromeric sequences using a library of 200 motifs to identify population stratification, finding that 177\% are significantly enriched in at least one continental population. As the number of telomere-to-telomere genomes increases, we anticipate FastSD to be a critical tool for rapid and accurate analysis of centromeric variation.

Talk/Poster Title: A Mecom—Cdk6 toggle switch governs hematopoietic stem-to-multipotent fate transitions via distinct multistable landscapes
Author(s): Jonathan A. Martinez, Anupam Dey, MeiLu McDermott, K. Lenhard Rudolph, Adam L. MacLean
Abstract: Hematopoietic stem cells are required to regenerate the blood system throughout life. We previously discovered that transitions between quiescent stem and multipotent progenitor states are controlled by mutual inhibition between Mecom and Cdk6, with upstream regulation from the insulin-like growth factor (IGF) signaling pathway. To investigate the dynamics of exit from quiescence and the stem-to-multipotent cell state transition, we modeled the Mecom-Cdk6 regulatory network via coupled nonlinear differential equations. Bifurcation analysis revealed that the model permits tetrastability, with two stable intermediate states, suggesting that stem cell exit from quiescence proceeds via multiple fine-scale transitions. Perturbation of Mecom self-activation reorganized the multistable landscape, producing two IGF-dependent landscapes with distinct geometries. At high IGF, transitions proceeded only through an intermediate state, whereas at low IGF, a distinct landscape emerged permitting direct transitions between cell states. Stochastic simulations and minimum action path analysis showed that the multipotent attractor is deep at high IGF, whereas low IGF promotes a transition to quiescence by stabilizing the stem cell state. Simulated pharmacological intervention via CDK4/6 inhibitors destabilized the multipotent state and favored transitions towards a more stem-like quiescent state. Together, these results demonstrate how IGF signaling, Mecom self-activation, and Cdk6 inhibition jointly shape early stem cell fate decisions by dictating the accessible cell states on multistable landscapes and the transition paths that connect them.

Talk/Poster Title: pyCurves: a modern DNA structural analyzer
Author(s): Jinsen Li, Remo Rohs
Abstract: DNA shape describes structural nuances of DNA structure, which provides a numerical linkage between nucleotide sequence, molecular recognition, and genome regulation. The legacy Curves program established an influential framework based on a globally optimized, deformable helical axis, but its requirements for manually prepared topology, specialized input formats, and legacy Fortran77 code create practical barriers to integration with contemporary structural workflows. Here, we present pyCurves, a Python reimplementation and extension of the Curves framework. pyCurves retains global curvilinear-axis optimization while replacing hand-derived derivatives with automatic differentiation and modern numerical optimization. It further integrates direct PDB/mmCIF input, automatic topology inference, modified-nucleotide handling, machine-readable output, and workflows for static structures and molecular-dynamics trajectories. In a PDB-scale benchmark, pyCurves expanded structural coverage while reproducing Curves and Curves+ parameters for canonical DNA within the precision of the legacy outputs. Comparisons between globally optimized and locally smoothed axes further showed that these constructions provide distinct, non-interchangeable descriptions of DNA shape. To extend the analysis beyond canonical Watson-Crick pairs, pyCurves introduces contact-geometry reference frames anchored to the interacting base edges. These frames reduce convention-associated rotational extremes and allow Hoogsteen and other noncanonical interactions to contribute consistently to helical-axis and groove analyses. For molecular-dynamics trajectories, a vectorized in-memory pipeline based on local-axis smoothing reduced processing time relative to the Curves+/Canal workflow. Together, pyCurves provides a compatible and extensible framework for analyzing DNA geometry across diverse structures and simulation scales.

Talk/Poster Title: Rethinking admixture mapping in terms of marginal coalescent trees
Author(s): Junjian "Janis" Liu, Michael "Doc" Edge
Abstract: Admixture mapping uses local ancestry to identify trait-associated genetic regions. Admixture mapping was adopted enthusiastically in the early 2000s because it required fewer markers than GWAS given the large extent of admixture linkage disequilibrium in recently admixed populations. There has been speculation that admixture mapping is poised for a return as multi-ancestry biobank resources become more common. However, admixture mapping requires assignment of haplotypes to discrete source populations. This conception of discrete populations has been argued to be a poor representation of much human population structure. Here, we re-cast admixture mapping in a continuous form by framing it in terms of variation in local relatedness. This conception does not require postulated discrete admixture groups. We show that a recent method for performing trait mapping using estimated marginal coalescent trees captures the local-ancestry associations that power admixture-mapping signals while also capturing loci that are more easily detected by GWAS than by admixture mapping. Thus, tree-based locus mapping has the potential to be a powerful overarching framework in the era of multi-ancestry studies of complex traits, one that captures the benefits of both admixture mapping and GWAS without requiring discrete ancestry groupings.

Talk/Poster Title: Novel demographic model of African American admixture applied to studying downstream biases of identity-by-descent inference
Author(s): Aydin Loid Karatas, Jazlyn Mooney
Abstract: Realistic demographic models connect historical processes with genetic variation in contemporary genomes, yet models of recent admixture often simplify the generation-by-generation processes that shape ancestry, relatedness, and diversity. Here, we address this gap by developing a generation-resolved model of four centuries of African American population history. Leveraging historical records and genealogical expectations, we parameterize per-generation population sizes, forced African importation, natural growth, continuing African and European admixture, and recent U.S. growth. The resulting simulations recapitulate realistic measures of ancestry and allelic diversity. To demonstrate the model's utility, we benchmarked identity-by-descent (IBD) inference under multiple genetic map choices and filtering schemes. IBD segments are shared portions of the genome that reflect the recent shared ancestry and are widely used to infer relatedness, population structure, and recent demographic history. We find that genetic map misspecification can substantially bias IBD inference, while genomic regions with low sequence complexity or poorly resolved recombination structure introduce systematic errors. IBD inference often performs best in the admixed population, supporting its utility for resolving recent, complex demographic histories. Method-specific trade-offs are evident: RaPID achieves higher accuracy when genetic maps are correctly specified and spurious segments are rigorously filtered, whereas hap-IBD is more robust to map misspecification and less stringent filtering. Altogether, our results provide a realistic framework for evaluating IBD-based inference and highlight considerations for demographic modeling and relatedness studies in admixed and non-model populations.

Talk/Poster Title: The biological plausibility of rare events in MD simulations of free DNA
Author(s): Dylan Kemmerer & Peijun Lin
Abstract: Elucidating the relationship between the dynamic three-dimensional shape of a DNA molecule and its constituent nucleotide sequence is critical for understanding the geometric grammar of protein-DNA interactions. Within a DNA molecule, the geometries of bases in an individual base-pair and of consecutive base-pairs are highly influenced by the surrounding nucleotide context. While obtaining crystal structures of every possible combination of nucleotide context to completely characterize the sequence-shape relationship is experimentally infeasible, well-parametrized molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provide a high-throughput alternative. For example, the recent hexABC dataset published by the Ascona B-DNA Consortium comprises 10-microsecond MD simulations containing every DNA hexamer and relates hexameric context with base-pair and consecutive base-pair geometry. Towards validating the hexABC dataset for future usage, we analyzed hexABC MD trajectory data with the software pyCurves to confirm that the data recapitulates known correlations between DNA shape parameters. Additionally, the longer timescale of each MD trajectory permits the observation of rare structural events, and we investigated their biological plausibility. These events included DNA melting, which involves the denaturation of hydrogen bonds between DNA strands, and Hoogsteen base-pairing, during which a purine must rotate around its glycosidic bond into a non-canonical conformation.

Talk/Poster Title: Expanding Protein-DNA Specificity Prediction through Structural Pseudo-Labeling
Author(s): Kalie Uberti, Kailin Liu, Viren Mehta, Wei Yu Tan, Tsu-Pei Chiu
Abstract: Understanding how transcription factors (TFs) recognize and bind DNA is fundamental to understanding gene regulation. DeepPBS predicts DNA-binding preferences as position weight matrices (PWMs) from protein-DNA structures, but its training is limited by the availability of experimental specificity measurements. We developed DeepPBS_SSL, a semi-supervised learning (SSL) framework that uses pseudo-labeling to incorporate structures lacking these measurements into training. Our results indicate that incorporating experimentally determined and AlphaFold 3-predicted structures substantially improves specificity prediction compared with supervised DeepPBS. We further investigate how SSL benefits vary across TF families and the potential for cross-family transfer. Using homeodomain and basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) TFs as case studies, we assess whether pseudo-labeling can compensate for missing experimental PWM supervision. For selected TFs, we use residue- and contact-level importance scores to examine how SSL changes the model's sensitivity to specific protein-DNA contacts and explore the potential biological relevance of these changes. We also explore an iterative workflow coupling DeepPBS_SSL with AlphaFold 3 to design candidate DNA-binding sites for selected TFs. DeepPBS_SSL expands training beyond experimentally labeled structures, improving specificity prediction while providing a foundation for investigating TF-DNA recognition mechanisms and guiding DNA-binding site design.

Talk/Poster Title: DeepLINK-T: deep learning inference for time series data using knockoffs and LSTM with applications to metagenomic data
Author(s): Kexin Wang, Wenxuan Zuo, Zifan Zhu, Yuxuan Du, Yi-Chun Yeh, Jed A. Fuhrman, Jinchi Lv, Yingying Fan, Fengzhu Sun
Abstract:
High-dimensional longitudinal time series data is prevalent across real world applications. Many such applications can be modeled as regression problems with high-dimensional time series covariates, for which deep learning is a popular and powerful fitting tool. Yet developing interpretable and reproducible deep-learning models remains challenging and underexplored. This study introduces a novel method, Deep Learning Inference using Knockoffs for Time series data (DeepLINK-T), to select significant time series variables in regression while controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) at a predetermined level. DeepLINK-T combines deep learning with knockoff inference to control FDR in feature selection for time series models, accommodating diverse feature distributions. It addresses
dependencies across time and features by leveraging a time-varying latent factor structure in covariates. Three key ingredients for DeepLINK-T are 1) a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) autoencoder or a stacked LSTM network for generating time series knockoff variables, 2) an LSTM prediction network using both original and knockoff variables, and 3) the application of the knockoffs framework for variable selection with FDR control. We establish theoretical guarantee and demonstrate empirically that DeepLINK-T controls FDR at the target level while achieving superior feature selection power to baseline methods across simulation studies and real data-based simulations. DeepLINK-T is further applied to three metagenomic datasets: longitudinal gut microbiome data of early infants, marine metagenomic time series data, and dietary glycans treatment time series data. Some important biological insights were obtained from these studies validating the practical utility and effectiveness, and underscoring the potential in real-world applications of DeepLINK-T.

Talk/Poster Title: Testing the Ability of AI Models to Capture Combinatorial Transcription Factor Action
Author(s):
Lucy Zhuo
PI: Judith Kribelbauer
Abstract: In regulatory regions of genomes, transcription factors recognize specific DNA sequences and regulate gene expression. Regulatory sequences have binding sites to allow for arrangements of numerous transcription factors (TFs) or combinations of them. Differing arrangements and sequences can influence regulatory activity. Modifying non-coding DNA can impact regulatory processes and the binding of transcription factors, which can alter gene expression. Modern technology such as AlphaGenome is a deep learning AI model which uses data to predict gene expression based on detecting underlying patterns. However, sequence changes and their regulatory effects are challenging to predict, largely because data is limited and derived from one human reference genome. In addition, there is no easy way to validate the accuracy of these AI models' predictions, as the experimental tools that can do so are not available at the necessary scale. Specifically, there is a lack of large scale experiments that can actually create new mutations while capturing how they impact combinatorial TF action. This project will use experimental data on the regulatory activity of synthetic regulatory regions, also known as enhancer regions, which contain either individual TFs or pairwise TFs to determine whether AI models have the capability to predict the activity of these synthetic sequences. The project will compare the impact of mutations on enhancer activity to predictions generated by modern AI models, such as AlphaGenome. Overall, this research may contribute to a better understanding of emerging AI tools and provide insight into its applications in the human genome.

Talk/Poster Title: Cell cycling throttles epithelial--mesenchymal transition
Author(s): MeiLu McDermott, Anupam Dey, Riddhee Mehta, & Adam L. MacLean
Abstract: Cell cycle phase is an understudied source of variation in gene expression. EMT is a case in point: this cell state transition that drives metastasis has been studied widely across tissue, stimulus, and microenvironmental conditions, yet cell cycle effects are routinely regressed out of single-cell EMT analyses. Here, we compare EMT between G1 and cycling (S/G2/M) cell states in two independent scRNA-seq datasets of TGF-$\beta$-stimulated MCF10A mammary epithelial cells (varying dose and timepoint). G1 cells consistently show higher expression of EMT genes and upregulated RNA velocities than cycling cells, with the strongest upregulation in G1 EMT intermediate states. Consistent with the go-or-grow hypothesis, EMT and cell cycle programs inversely correlate; moreover, this anticorrelation extends to RNA velocity and strengthens with TGF-$\beta$ dose. We identify a 77-gene G1-specific EMT signature enriched for actin cytoskeletal and extracellular matrix genes that would otherwise be lost by regressing out cell cycle effects. This gene set prompts the hypothesis that, unconstrained by the cytoskeletal demands of mitosis, G1 cells have greater capacity to execute EMT. Further, we developed an EMT gene regulatory model coupled with a cell cycle module, and found through simulation that the model recapitulated this inverse EMT---cell cycle relationship. Using this model, we predict that cycle-selective chemotherapy enriches for the G1 intermediate state, which has high metastatic potential. Cell cycle phase thus ought not be regressed out of EMT states, given its influence on EMT.

Talk/Poster Title: Inferring Selection on Polygenic Traits in British Individuals using Marginal Coalescent Trees
Author(s): Obadiah Mulder, Michael "Doc" Edge
Abstract: Selection on complex traits is difficult to detect using classic methods. Variants affecting highly polygenic traits generally have small effect sizes and selection at any given locus is usually weak. Several recent methods have addressed this problem by using genome-wide association study (GWAS) information to construct polygenic scores for traits of interest and then testing these polygenic scores for evidence of selection. One set of methods in this family, due to Edge and Coop (2019), uses marginal coalescent trees to estimate the historical time course of population-mean polygenic scores, giving information about both the timing and strength of selection. Further work by Peng and colleagues (2025) demonstrated that the marginal coalescent trees estimated by SINGER perform very well at this task. However, there have been few efforts to assess selection in empirical data using these tools. Here, we use allelic effect size estimates to form population-mean polygenic scores for height, and we test for evidence of directional selection among the ancestors of the British (GBR) subset of 1000 Genomes Project participants.

Talk/Poster Title: Generating Sequence-Specific DNA Conformational Ensembles at Molecular-Dynamics Quality
Author(s): Peijun Lin, Jinsen Li, Remo Rohs*
Abstract:
DNA shape, the geometry of base pairs and grooves, enables proteins read sequence without touching the bases. Current method such as Deep DNAshape predict one average value per position, but DNA in solution is a fluctuating ensemble. Different DNA shape feature correlated with each other, and neighboring positions move together. Molecular dynamics (MD) captures this, but costs weeks of GPU time per sequence. Here we present a sequence-conditioned flow-matching model that generates DNA conformational ensembles directly. It samples rigid-base shape parameters at every position and rebuild the DNA 3D structures from the shape parameters. 

On held-out sequences, the generated ensemble is as close to MD as one MD replica is to another. This holds for every shape feature, including the bimodal CpG step, for shape features correlation, for the dominant collective motions, and for rebuilt 3D structures. It also holds beyond the training data source, on four independent MD datasets run with different water models, software and lengths. As for the speed, one 10-µs-equivalent ensemble takes 2 seconds instead of an estimated 19 GPU-days, a near million-fold speedup. This work opens questions that prediction model cannot reach: how rare a given conformation is, how DNA flanking a bound protein responds when the interface is held fixed, and which sequences best encode a target shape in their ensemble.

Talk/Poster Title: Single-molecule CTCF occupancy and zinc-finger engagement states revealed by Fiber-seq
Author(s): Peiyu Shi, Geoffrey Fudenberg
Abstract: CTCF and cohesin are major organizers of three-dimensional genome architecture. Cohesin extrudes chromatin loops, and DNA-bound CTCF acts as a directional boundary that can pause or retain cohesin. Yet CTCF sites are neither constitutively occupied nor perfectly impermeable to cohesin, making both CTCF binding and boundary activity probabilistic. The molecular determinants underlying these two layers of heterogeneity remain incompletely understood. Here, we analyze Fiber-seq, a single-molecule chromatin footprinting approach, to quantify CTCF occupancy and zinc-finger (ZF)-DNA engagement on individual native DNA molecules. We find that CTCF occupancy is jointly shaped by sequence affinity, CpG methylation, and local chromatin context, with allele-specific binding providing an internal validation of these determinants. Beyond occupancy, single-molecule protection patterns reveal recurrent CTCF ZF-DNA engagement states whose relative abundance varies across genomic loci and is influenced by local sequence context. Importantly, engagement-state composition provides additional information about RAD21 enrichment, insulation strength, and chromatin loop strength beyond CTCF occupancy. Together, these results establish two quantitative dimensions of endogenous CTCF binding: occupancy determines how frequently a CTCF barrier is present, whereas the DNA-engagement state of bound CTCF provides a second layer associated with its functional effectiveness as a cohesin boundary.

Talk/Poster Title: CLASH (Chromatin Loop Across-sample Score Harmonizer) quantifies the relative contributions of genetic variation, methylation, and CTCF occupancy on chromatin loop strength across individuals
Author(s): Valmik Ranparia, The Human Genome Structural Variation Consortium, Geoffrey Fudenberg, Mark Chaisson
Abstract: Three-dimensional genome organization constrains the regulatory interactions that govern vital cellular processes. Chromatin loops are key features of genome folding, yet how genetic and epigenetic variation influences differential loop formation across individuals remains unclear. To investigate this, we combined high-resolution Hi-C, Fiber-seq, near telomere-to-telomere phased assemblies, and m⁵C methylation maps across five lymphoblastoid cell lines. Next, we developed CLASH (Chromatin Loop Across-sample Score Harmonizer) to harmonize loop calls across samples and enable robust comparisons of loop strengths across individuals. Using CLASH, we characterized the contributions of CTCF occupancy, sequence, and epigenetic variation to differential loop formation, demonstrating that ~75% of naturally occurring differential loops between individuals are associated with changes in at least one of these three features. Together, we present a multimodal dataset and computational approach to facilitate the study of 3D genome structure across human populations.

Talk/Poster Title: Toward a Biophysics-Informed Framework for Enhancer-Promoter Interaction
Author(s): Md Rownok Zahan Ratul, Geoffrey Fudenberg
Abstract:
Gene expression depends on both local regulatory sequence and communication between distal enhancers and their target promoters. Long-context sequence models such as AlphaGenome and Borzoi can predict genomic signals, but whether they capture the experimentally observed rules of enhancer-promoter communication remains unclear.
We benchmark these models using controlled perturbation experiments at the Sox2 and Car2 loci in mouse embryonic stem cells from Zuin et al. and Hansen et al. These experiments examine enhancer relocation, enhancer-promoter distance, regulatory element combinations, and changes to chromosomal architecture. By recreating these perturbations in silico, we assess whether the models reproduce observed transcriptional direction, magnitude, distance dependence, insulation, and combinatorial enhancer effects.
We explore a biophysics-informed framework that decomposes expression into basal promoter activity, enhancer activity, enhancer-promoter contact, and promoter responsiveness. This work uses experimentally controlled benchmarks to identify what current sequence models capture about distal regulation and to guide the development of more interpretable models of enhancer-promoter communication.

Talk/Poster Title: Retained Ancestry Switches as Signals of  Effective Population Size in Admixed Populations
Author(s): Shengmiao Huang, Shirin Nataneli, Roshni Patel, and Jazlyn Mooney
Abstract: Admixed genomes contain ancestry switches generated by recombination and shaped by drift over time. Here, we develop a retained switch model to account for the loss of observable ancestry switches under drift. We use simulations to show that the model fits better with a sufficiently large population size, and is most informative within a limited (G/2Ne) range. Maximum-likelihood estimation of recent (Ne) remains unstable across many settings. Further investigation is needed to improve inference from retained ancestry switches.

Talk/Poster Title: Incorporating protein conformational heterogeneity into structure-based models of transcription factor specificity
Author(s): Alexandra M. Shewchuk, Tsu-Pei Chiu, Jinsen Li, Remo Rohs
Abstract:
Transcription factors regulate gene expression through dynamic interactions with DNA that depend on conformational flexibility in both partners. Because specificity emerges from coupled conformational ensembles and involves both direct chemical contacts (base readout) and structural recognition (shape readout), prediction requires models that move beyond static structures. Molecular dynamics captures these effects but does not scale; recent methods such as BioEmu predict protein conformational ensembles at MD-level accuracy, yet protein-DNA complex dynamics have not been incorporated.

We built a scalable pipeline coupling BioEmu-derived ensembles to DeepPBS, an interpretable geometric deep learning framework for predicting binding specificity from structure, and applied it across 12 TF systems. This yields a direct measurement of how much predicted specificity depends on which conformation of a protein one happens to have.

Across 701 bound conformations, predicted specificity varies substantially more between conformations of the same protein than between independently trained models, establishing quantitatively that a crystal structure is a point estimate of a conformational distribution. Ensemble averaging recovers most of the crystal's prediction, showing the conformers sample coherently around the bound state.

Furthermore, because every conformer inherits its protein's experimental motif as a shared label, the network learns conformational invariance, with across-conformer variance dropping in 11 of 12 systems. This demonstrates that performance limit stems from how the training labels are assigned, rather than the quality of the ensembles or the capacity of the network, and points directly at per-conformation labeling as the next step.

Talk/Poster Title: Comparative exploration of gene-based and k-mer based features for predicting antimicrobial resistance
Author(s): Shreyash Sinha, Fengzhu Sun
Abstract:
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an ever-growing threat to public health, with a recent study forecasting that bacterial AMR could directly lead to 39 million deaths between 2025 and 2050. Advances in whole-genome sequencing have enabled the development of machine learning approaches for predicting AMR phenotypes directly from bacterial genomes. However, extracting highly informative and generalizable genomic features from bacterial sequences remains a major challenge. 
Two widely used genomic feature types for AMR prediction are gene-based features and k-mer based features. Gene-based methods predict resistance based on known antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) or gene clusters and are highly interpretable. However, they are limited by the quality of curated reference databases and could miss novel resistance mechanisms and non-coding resistant variants. k-mer based methods provide a reference-free prediction approach. However, the use of long k-mers is computationally challenging because it produces sparse, high-dimensional feature matrices containing many correlated features.
In this study, we compare different feature choices for training machine learning methods such as random forest and extreme gradient boosting for AMR prediction. Preliminary results demonstrate that statistically filtered long k-mer based features show high predictive power. We further investigate whether biologically informed features and reference-free features can be combined to provide complementary information for improving prediction accuracy, generalizability and interpretability

Talk/Poster Title: Using Weak SINDy to Learn the PDEs of Tumor Growth from Noisy, Agent-based Snapshots
Author(s): Sriram Seshadri, Adam MacLean
Abstract: ABMs (Agent-based models) are useful models for representing tumor cells as agents that divide, migrate, and respond to nutrient fields, but are difficult to interpret and expensive to simulate. We hypothesized that a set of continuum PDEs can be discovered from noisy ABM data without the ground truth of the ABM update rules or the underlying nutrient field PDEs. We ran 65 PhysiCell simulations of a tumor in a hypoxic environment that, when coarse-grained, closely mirror the growth of 3 outwardly expanding annuluses corresponding to normoxic, hypoxic, and necrotic cell densities. We also introduce depth below the tumor ring to capture the unobserved oxygen gradient. We then employed Weak SINDy (Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics) which entails weak-form regression on a library of candidate terms to learn a coefficient matrix, followed by rollout refinement and model selection. By penalizing high complexity and rollout error, we obtained a 10-term partial differential equation that predicts tumor growth with 39% error, compared to 105% for standard SINDy. We were able to infer biological meaning from these learned PDEs such as oxygen-dependent switching thresholds, drift and proliferation-driven flow.

Talk/Poster Title: Leveraging Runs of Homozygosity to Identify Recessive Complex Trait Architecture
Author(s): Tessa Ferrari, Arun Durvasula, Jazlyn Mooney
Abstract: Runs of homozygosity (ROH) are continuous stretches of homozygous genotypes created when haplotypes are inherited identically-by-descent from both parents. Rare variants within an ROH are inherited in their homozygous form, which unmasks potentially deleterious recessive variation that would otherwise be obscured in heterozygotes. Longer ROH are associated with more recent inbreeding and consanguinity, and variants within them likely have not experienced selection. Thus, ROH are enriched for deleterious variation and could be associated with complex diseases and traits. Previous empirical studies have found associations between genomic ROH burden (FROH) and complex phenotypes as evidence for recessive complex trait architecture. Reliably identifying recessive traits is an important first step to closing a long-standing gap in typical genome-wide association (GWA) methodology, since additive GWA models are underpowered for detecting rare recessive variation. However, the mechanism by which these FROH-trait associations occur in structured populations is not yet fully understood. There is no consensus on an appropriate model to reliably capture the signal while simultaneously correcting for structure. Here, we simulated traits under various architectures using multiple analytical and population genetics simulation frameworks and conducted FROH-trait association tests. We then evaluated their ability to accurately capture signals of trait recessivity in order to elucidate the nuanced relationship between ROH, complex traits, and population dynamics. As expected, we find that as trait narrow-sense heritability increases, the power to detect recessive traits increases. However, under simulation frameworks using more realistic population dynamics, we find decreased power and a false discovery rate that deviates from expectations, especially in more structured populations. Finally, we implement FROH-trait association tests in 3 empirical populations from the UK BioBank across 22 health-associated complex traits. In a White British population and South Asian population, we detect 6 shared trait associations (e.g. BMI, Vitamin D, etc.) as well as 6 population-specific ones (e.g. LDL in White British, Hemoglobin in South Asian). We detect no associations in a Black Caribbean population, perhaps due to sample size or complex structure from recent admixture.

Talk/Poster Title: Interplay of diffusive and active motion governs tension-dependent loop extrusion by cohesin
Author(s): Maxime Tortora
Abstract: Cohesin-mediated loop extrusion constitutes a crucial process for the regulation of chromosome folding and gene expression. A rapidly-growing body of in vitro experiments suggest that cohesin molecular motor activity is finely modulated by both chemical and mechanical cues, whose interplay holds important implications in living cells for development and disease. Yet, biophysical models capable of accurately and efficiently capturing the breadth of reported cohesin behaviors, along with their impacts on DNA spatio-temporal organisation, remain lacking. Here, building on multiple experimental observations of single-cohesin dynamics, we introduce a minimalistic description of cohesin based on the general framework of jump-diffusion processes. We show that the finite stall force of cohesin naturally emerges from the conjunction of active, directional extrusion moves with passive, stochastic drift. The tension-dependent competition between these two orthogonal modes of motion gives rise to highly-heterogeneous cohesin kinetics featuring extrusion, translocation, and loop slipping phases, in striking agreement with in vitro observations. The different force regimes underlying these distinct dynamics are predicted to depend sensitively on both buffer composition and nucleosomal content, thus providing mechanistic insight into the surprising variability of cohesin kinetics reported across experimental conditions. This jump-diffusion model is fully parametrized using available single-molecule measurements, and may be seamlessly integrated into GPU-accelerated molecular dynamics. Hence, our approach allows for quantitative simulations of force-dependent extrusion in both DNA curtain assays in vitro and in the context of native chromatin for genome folding predictions in nucleo, bridging these previously disparate extrusion contexts under a unified numerical and theoretical formalism.

Talk/Poster Title: DNA breathing and shape encode distinct mechanisms of transcription factor binding
Author(s): Tsu-Pei Chiu, Wei Yu Tang, and Remo Rohs
Abstract: Interactions between transcription factors (TFs) and DNA play a key role in regulating gene expression. While these interactions are often viewed primarily as recognition of DNA sequence motifs, several studies have shown the limitation of this approach and highlighted the impact of physical properties of DNA. Prior studies have supported the importance of DNA shape features as determinant of TF-DNA recognition. Another physical property is DNA breathing, the spontaneous and transient opening of double-stranded DNA through thermal motions, which has not been systematically examined. We analyzed in vitro TF-DNA binding data and found that DNA breathing features in motif regions are correlated with binding affinity, highlighting a role of locally and temporally melted DNA. Here, we compared contributions of DNA breathing and shape to TF binding. These analyses suggest that DNA breathing provides sequence-dependent information related to DNA structure not fully captured by DNA shape. Extending the analysis to ChIP-seq data, we found that breathing features are associated with TF binding in vivo, although the direction and magnitude of these associations vary across TFs. Our results support DNA breathing as an additional physical feature contributing to TF-DNA interactions alongside DNA sequence motifs and DNA shape.

Talk/Poster Title: DeepPBS-AF3: Bridging structure- and sequence-based models of protein-DNA binding specificity with AlphaFold 3
Author(s): Wei Yu Tang, Jinsen Li, Peijun Lin, Kalie Uberti, Tsu-Pei Chiu, and Remo Rohs
Abstract: Predicting DNA-binding specificity of a transcription factor (TF) is a challenging yet essential task for understanding gene regulation. While sequence-based models utilize abundant high-throughput binding data, the diversity of protein folds and binding-associated conformational changes motivate approaches that use 3D structural information. Previous work, DeepPBS, addresses this by predicting binding specificity as a position weight matrix (PWM) directly from protein-DNA complexes, by encoding physicochemical and geometric interactions. Its training, however, is heavily limited by the scarcity of experimental TF-DNA co-crystal structures. Here, we introduce DeepPBS-AF3, which leverages AlphaFold 3 (AF3) to generate structural inputs for TFs that lack experimental complexes. This approach enables DeepPBS-AF3 to be trained on AF3-predicted complexes and extends its applicability to binding specificity prediction with sequence inputs. When trained on AF3-predicted structures, DeepPBS-AF3 demonstrates greater accuracy and generalizability over DeepPBS. Furthermore, we present a workflow that predicts binding specificity for a TF without a known binding DNA sequence. Together, our results establish structure prediction as a viable approach to overcome the scarcity of experimental structures in structure-based prediction of binding specificity, with potential extension to other applications such as predicting binding affinity and binding sites.

Talk/Poster Title: When DL-Based Prescreening Meets Synthon-Based Docking: Target-Adapting PharmacoNet via MEL-Steered Correction
Author(s): Wenjin Liu, Yongchan Hong, Woojin Lee, Thomas Ku, Emily Nguyen, Ao Xu, Vsevolod Katritch
Abstract: As chemical libraries expand into the trillions of molecules, Virtual SYNthon Hierarchical Enumeration Screening (V-SYNTHES) has emerged as a leading strategy for making gigascale virtual screening computationally tractable. In V-SYNTHES, a Minimal Enumeration Library (MEL) of chemical fragments is docked against a target first, and only the top-scoring fragments are expanded into full ligands for large-scale docking. However, among the large number of comparably well-docked fragments, only a small fraction can be expanded under a fixed docking budget, leaving most similarly promising fragments unexplored. General-purpose prescreening tools can be adopted to address this constraint, reallocating the same docking budget across a larger pool of fragments' enumerated full ligands by their proxy score. However, such tools are applied without accounting for target-specific pocket environments. One such method, PharmacoNet, predicts interaction hotspots from a protein structure and ranks candidates via graph matching against a fixed set of interaction-type weights. We recognize that V-SYNTHES's initial fragment-docking step, ordinarily used only for selection of best fragments for expansion, already reveals which of these hotspots and interaction types a given pocket actually favors, and we can recover this signal to fine-tune PharmacoNet accordingly. We introduce MEL-Steered PharmacoNet, a parameter-efficient adaptation framework that specializes PharmacoNet to a given target through two composable mechanisms: (i) empirical density-map steering of predicted pharmacophore hotspots, and (ii) empirical fine-tuning of interaction-type scoring weights. Across three structurally distinct GPCR targets (CB2, GPR91, 5-HT2AR), MEL-Steered PharmacoNet achieves substantial enrichment factor EF\({100}\) gains over a random baseline, and improves EF\({100}\) over PharmacoNet. The fitted per-target weights further reveal distinct, chemically interpretable interaction profiles that PharmacoNet's generic fixed weights fail to capture. These results show that fragment-docking data already generated by the standard V-SYNTHES pipeline can adapt a general-purpose pharmacophore prescreening method to an individual target, significantly improving its performance while retaining its ultra-fast screening ability, with no additional experimental data or model retraining.

Talk/Poster Title: VHSeek: Biology foundation model-based virus representations revealing virus host associations
Author(s): Wei Liu, Yuqiu Wang, Jed A. Fuhrman, Hui Li, Le Song, Gauri G. Rao, Fengzhu Sun
Abstract:
Virus-host association prediction is fundamental to virus-related disease control
and phage therapy, yet many existing tools require candidate-host genome
sequences, which may be unavailable for some eukaryotic hosts or impractical
to search at the scale of large virome studies. We present VHSeek, a supervised
virus-host association predictor that integrates DNA- and protein-derived viral
representations. VHSeek combines nucleotide representations from AIDO.DNA
and protein representations from ESM2 to learn virus-host association patterns,
and then transfers predictions through known host taxonomies from lower to
higher ranks. During inference, VHSeek uses viral sequence data and known host
taxonomies, without host sequence data. Compared with iPHoP, the state-ofthe-
art baseline evaluated in this study, VHSeek improves genus-level maximum
F1 score (Fmax), Top-1 accuracy, and area under the precision-recall curve
(AUPR) by 12%, 19%, and 27%, respectively. Confidence thresholding enables
abstention and reduces false discoveries. On the processed IMG/VR v4.1 metagenomic
collection, VHSeek expands effective host coverage from 36.5% to 64.5% using a validation-calibrated confidence threshold. VHSeek prioritizes candidate
viruses and reservoir hosts with potential human health impacts, including
multi-host hypotheses in which one virus may be associated with humans and
additional hosts (e.g., Saboya virus with Homo sapiens and Culicidae) not
currently captured in the dataset.

Talk/Poster Title: Structure-based discovery of prostaglandin D2 receptor 1 modulators via virtual screening of trillion-scale chemical space
Author(s): Woojin Lee, Aleksey Raskovalov, Zixin Zhang, Donggyun Kim, Anastasiia Sadybekov, Penghao Song, Joshua S. Ho, Gye Won Han, Vadim Cherezov, Vsevolod Katritch
Abstract: The prostaglandin D2 receptor 1 (DP1), a member of the prostanoid G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) family, is a key regulator of allergic responses, sleep regulation, immune modulation, and vasodilation. Here, we investigated to identify novel small molecules that modulate DP1 activity by binding to its orthosteric pocket. Using the modular synthon-based computational platform, Virtual SYNthon Hierarchical Enumeration Screening (V-SYNTHES), we screened a three-trillion-compound Enamine xREAL make-on-demand chemical space against DP1 cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures and prioritized 269 candidates. Of these, 209 compounds were synthesized with a 78% success rate and validated through in vitro functional assays. This effort identified 20 antagonists and 3 agonists with the best potencies of IC50 = 441 nM and EC50 = 1.3 µM, respectively. Furthermore, the cryo-EM structure of DP1 bound to one of our leading antagonists confirms the computationally predicted binding mode and highlights key ligand-receptor interactions. These findings establish a foundation for ongoing hit-to-lead optimization and the structure-based design of next-generation DP1 modulators as well as a promising starting point for the development of potent therapeutics.

Talk/Poster Title: Replicated chromosome folding records cohesin turnover, transport, and encounters
Author(s): Xingchi Yan, Maxime Tortora, Anton Goloborodko, Geoff Fudenberg
Abstract: The cohesin complex physically links sister chromatids after DNA replication. These cohesin linkages must be maintained for many hours for faithful chromosome segregation and DNA repair. Cohesin interacts with multiple rapidly-exchanging cofactors, including SORORIN, which is often described as a ‘molecular lock' for cohesin on chromatin. How such transient SORORIN binding can protect cohesin over much longer timescales remains mechanistically unclear. Furthermore, how loop-extruding cohesins interact with and influence the positioning of sister-linking cohesins remains largely unknown. Here we show how sister chromatid folding over time and after perturbations encodes information sufficient to resolve underlying mechanisms of cohesin maintenance. Repeated transient sequestration by SORORIN enables long-lasting protection yet acts as a quantitative modulator, rather than a binary switch for cohesion maintenance. Prolonging cohesin residence time by WAPL depletion exposes additional mechanisms shaping sister chromatid conformation, including pushing of sister-linking cohesins and diffusion of loop-extruding cohesins. Together, these results reveal how transient cofactor interactions regulate long-lived cohesin maintenance and establish sister chromosome organization as a quantitative readout of otherwise hidden molecular mechanisms.

Talk/Poster Title: iLV-HD: Reconstructing microbial dynamics from high-dimensional compositional time series
Author(s): Yue Huang, Kexin Wang, Fengzhu Sun
Abstract: Microbial time series are often measured as relative abundances across hundreds of taxa, leaving too few observations to estimate their interactions directly. We developed iLV-HD to model these data by grouping taxa with similar temporal patterns and fitting regularized Lotka-Volterra dynamics to the resulting subgroups. We compared an L1-regularized model (Auto-L1) with a variant that explicitly removes weak interactions (Sparse-v2). In a ten-species simulation, both methods reproduced the observed trajectories with very low error, but neither recovered the generating interaction matrix accurately. We then evaluated the methods against four comparison implementations on two densely sampled microbial time series using repeated withheld-time-point reconstruction. Auto-L1 and Sparse-v2 performed similarly on a human gut series, whereas Auto-L1 achieved the lowest error and greatest stability on a coastal plankton series. Selecting the regularization strength by grid search improved fits to empirical data at substantial computational cost. Adding four measured environmental variables did not improve the fit to a separate coastal time series. These results show that subgroup-based modeling can reconstruct high-dimensional compositional dynamics, while interaction estimates require separate validation. The framework provides a practical approach to analyzing microbial time series when absolute abundances are unavailable.

Talk/Poster Title: Spatial cell circuits reveal communication pattern in the breast cancer TME with single-cell and spatial transcriptomics
Author(s): Yingtong Liu, Xiaojun Wu, Alexander H. Lee, Evanthia T. Roussos Torres, Adam L. MacLean
Abstract: The tumor microenvironment (TME) comprises diverse cell populations whose interactions shape tumor progression. Cell-cell communication (CCC) analysis using scRNA-seq enables the inference of ligand-receptor-mediated signaling networks and the identification of cell-state-specific interactions. We developed a computational framework to extract and compare local CCC motifs based on their topology, cellular composition, and ligand-receptor signaling patterns. Prior work has shown that motif analysis of CCC networks can reveal recurrent signaling circuits associated with biological conditions. However, scRNA-seq lacks spatial context, limiting its ability to capture spatially constrained interactions. Here, we extend CCC motif analysis to spatial transcriptomics by leveraging CellNEST, a graph attention network (GAT)-based framework, to model spatially informed cell-cell interactions. Applied to breast cancer datasets across multiple time points, this approach enables the characterization of spatial CCC patterns and the exploration of motif organization under spatial constraints. Application to spatial breast cancer datasets reveals a heterogeneous landscape of communication motifs that can nevertheless be organized into recurrent groups with shared structural and cellular features.

Talk/Poster Title: Computational modeling links lymphatic endothelial signaling dynamics to junction state and predicts lymphatic responses to obesity
Author(s): Yiping Jia, Silvia Gonzalez Nieves, Vincenza Cifarelli, Stacey Finley
Abstract: Lymphatic endothelial junctions switch between continuous zippered and discontinuous button configurations to control entry of fluid, cells, and macromolecules into initial lymphatics. However, this control has been defined only through discrete perturbations and steady-state readouts, leaving unresolved how the magnitude and duration of signaling map onto the junction state. To address this gap, we developed a computational model of lymphatic endothelial signaling mediated by the growth factor, VEGF-A, simulating a heterogeneous population of cells. We trained and validated the model using published experimental data from cultured human dermal lymphatic endothelial cells (HDLECs). We defined the “zippering propensity”, a time-integrated quantitative metric that summarizes junction-stabilizing signaling over time. The model predicted that VEGF-A transiently increased zippering propensity, and sensitivity analysis identified the RAC1-RhoA antagonism and dephosphorylation rates as the principal regulators of response duration. To test whether this control is conserved across lymphatic beds, we analyzed published single-cell RNA sequencing data from mesenteric and epididymal LECs of mice fed normal chow or a high-fat diet (HFD). Our model predicts that transcriptional changes associated with HFD reshape VEGF-A-VEGFR signaling in an LEC subpopulation-specific manner. All modeled subpopulations are predicted to enter the zippered-like state following VEGF-A stimulation; what differs is how long that response duration persists and how the response duration is affected by the VEGF-A dose, with divergent outcomes for mesenteric versus epididymal capillary LECs, and for capillary versus collector LECs within the epididymal bed. These results provide a quantitative framework for predicting how junctions respond to VEGF-A stimulation and to disease-associated molecular change.

Talk/Poster Title: MACONi: a marker- and composition-aware framework for meta-Hi-C contact normalization
Author(s): Yangyang Liu, Fengzhu Sun
Abstract: High-throughput sequencing has enabled the systematic characterization of complex microbial communities. Metagenomic Hi-C (meta-Hi-C) further extends this capability by capturing physical interactions between DNA molecules, empowering metagenomic binning, host-plasmid linkage, and microbial interaction analysis. However, the utility of meta-Hi-C data is often confounded by coverage biases, spurious interspecies cross-talk, and compositional artifacts, which collectively limit accurate downstream inference. Here, we introduce MACONi, marker- and composition-aware framework for meta-Hi-C contact normalization. By integrating contact-depth normalization with marker-gene exclusivity and sequence-composition similarity, MACONi effectively filters out biologically incompatible contacts while preserving bona fide genome-consistent signals. Our comprehensive evaluations on both simulated and complex environmental datasets demonstrate that MACONi substantially enhances downstream binning, yielding a significantly greater number of high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs). Ultimately, MACONi provides a general approach to extract reliable biological insights from meta-Hi-C data, advancing high-resolution, genome-centric studies of microbiomes.

Talk/Poster Title: OMP loops contribute to phage-host infection across multiple bacterial genera
Author(s): Yuhao Zhang, Wei Liu, Fengzhu Sun
Abstract: Predicting whether a bacteriophage can infect a particular bacterial strain requires genomic features that distinguish susceptible from resistant hosts. Outer-membrane proteins (OMPs) offer a biologically motivated source of such features because some phages recognize surface-exposed OMP loops. Here, we tested OMP-loop sequences from curated panels across datasets from five bacterial genera: Escherichia, Klebsiella, Vibrio, Alteromonas, and Pseudomonas. We use OMP loops to represent the extracellular amino-acid segments extracted from these panels. Each loop was represented separately, preserving its identity and sequence variation, and combined with candidate phage receptor-binding proteins (RBPs) in a model trained for each dataset. OMP-loop models retained predictive information when related Escherichia host strains were held out together, with performance similar to full-length OMP and sugar-associated protein controls. Across the three Klebsiella analysis settings assembled from published collections, OMP-loop and sugar-associated protein inputs gave similar performance. In Alteromonas under the Cartesian split, OMP loops paired with genome-screened RBPs gave the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and average precision (AP) among the four tested configurations. Under host-lineage holdout, the sugar-associated protein control gave higher mean performance. Performance in other genera depended on the dataset and evaluation split. Masking ranked OMP inputs by the resulting decrease in AUROC, highlighting Escherichia LamB, OmpF, and BtuB inputs with experimental receptor precedents. Masking effects were evaluated across five seeds for every dataset, with variation across models and datasets. Host-phage synergy, defined as a pair's predicted score beyond the average effects of its host and phage, revealed dataset-dependent patterns of compatibility. These results support OMP loops as an intermediate representation between narrowly specified receptor features and proteome-wide inputs, with individual sequence features that can be related to receptor biology.

Talk/Poster Title: Single-cell QTL mapping of RNA kinetics reveals cell-type-specific genetic regulation of transcriptional dynamics
Author(s): Yumin Wang (University of Southern California), Zixuan Eleanor Zhang (University of Pennsylvania), Pejman Mohammadi (University of Washington School of Medicine, Seattle Children's Research Institute), Brunilda Balliu (University of California, Los Angeles), Nicholas Mancuso (Keck School of Medicine, University of Southern California)
Abstract:
Population-scale single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) offers an unprecedented opportunity to dissect genetic influences on gene regulation at cellular resolution. However, most existing single-cell expression QTL (sc-eQTL) analyses have been performed on total RNA abundance, obscuring how genetic variation modulates underlying transcriptional dynamics. Recent advances in biophysical models of transcriptional bursting enable estimation of kinetic parameters (burst size, and splicing and degradation rates relative to transcription) yet their genetic determinants remain largely unexplored.
Here, we introduce a single-cell kinetic QTL (sc-kQTL) framework to map genetic effects on RNA dynamics in a cell-type-specific manner. Using population-scale scRNA-seq data from 982 individuals (OneK1K; ~1.27 million immune cells across 14 cell types), we quantified nascent and mature RNA via kallisto|bustools and inferred gene-level kinetic parameters using the biVI model. Because these parameters are correlated, we first adjusted the kinetic phenotypes for demographic, genetic, and technical covariates and then applied FastGxC to decompose the residual variation into burst-size-specific, relative-splicing-specific, relative-degradation-specific, and shared components. We subsequently performed cis-kQTL mapping of these components using tensorQTL.
We identified 126,294 significant index sc-kQTL associations, demonstrating pervasive genetic regulation of transcriptional kinetics. Burst-size-specific sc-kQTLs were most abundant (36.1%), followed by relative-splicing-specific (30.9%), relative-degradation-specific (22.1%), and shared-component sc-kQTLs (10.9%). kGenes showed substantial sharing across kinetic components and related immune cell types, alongside component- and cell-type-specific effects. In the independent CLUES cohort, substantial proportions of associations replicated at FDR < 0.05, with replication rates ranging from 24.9% to 55.0% across kinetic components and matched cell types; replicated associations also exhibited directionally consistent genetic effects.
Lead kVariants were concentrated near transcription start sites, while relative-degradation-specific variants showed an additional peak near gene ends. Functional enrichment analyses revealed a broadly shared regulatory architecture involving promoter-proximal, untranslated, coding, and splice-related annotations, with quantitative differences across kinetic components. Relative-splicing QTL genes showed the strongest evolutionary constraint across multiple gene-constraint measures. Only 17.2-26.4% of kGenes overlapped with JAX sc-eQTL eGenes, indicating that kinetic traits capture regulatory variation beyond steady-state expression. Among 26,218 overlapping kGene-eGene cases, 61.0% supported a shared causal variant (coloc PP.H4 > 0.8).
Together, our framework extends sc-eQTL analysis by identifying the kinetic processes through which genetic variants influence RNA regulation, providing a mechanistic layer for interpreting regulatory variation and disease biology.

Talk/Poster Title: Benchmarking alignment strategies for Hi-C reads in metagenomic Hi-C data
Author(s): Yuqiu Wang, Wenxuan Zuo, Jiawei Huang, Fengzhu Sun, Yuxuan Du
Abstract: Metagenomics combined with High-throughput Chromosome Conformation Capture (Hi-C) provides a powerful approach to study microbial communities by linking genomic content with spatial interactions. Hi-C complements shotgun sequencing by revealing taxonomic composition, functional interactions, and genomic organization within a single sample. However, aligning Hi-C reads to metagenomic contigs is challenging due to variable insert sizes of Hi-C paired-end reads, multi-species complexity, and gaps in assemblies. Although several benchmark studies have evaluated general alignment tools and Hi-C data alignment, none have specifically focused on metagenomic Hi-C data. We evaluated seven alignment strategies commonly used in Hi-C analyses: BWA MEM -5SP, BWA MEM default, BWA aln default, Bowtie2 default, Bowtie2 -very-sensitive-local, Minimap2 default, and Chromap Hi-C default. We benchmarked these tools on one synthetic dataset and seven real-world environments. Performance was assessed based on the number of inter-contig Hi-C read pairs and their impact on downstream tasks, such as binning quality. We show that BWA MEM -5SP generally outperformed all other tools across most environments in terms of inter-contig read pairs and binning quality, followed by BWA MEM default. Chromap and Minimap2, while less effective in these metrics, demonstrated the highest computational efficiency.

Talk/Poster Title: Exploring the Interplay between NMD-Regulatory Variation and Somatic Mutational States in Cancer
Author(s): Zijin Xiang, Liang Chen
Abstract: Nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) regulates transcript stability and may shape the consequences of somatic alterations in cancer. We asked whether genetic variants linked to NMD influence how somatic mutations relate to tumor gene expression and patient survival. Using data from The Cancer Genome Atlas, we analyzed NMD-associated genotypes, somatic mutation scores, gene expression, and overall survival. We used elastic-net regression to select predictors, followed by regression analysis and permutation testing. Among 2,174 genes, we identified 225 with potential interactions between NMD-associated variants and somatic scores. For these genes, the relationship between somatic scores and expression differed across genotypes. These genes also showed greater cancer-cell dependency in DepMap, even after accounting for expression levels. Survival analyses identified 22 genes with potential interactions. These findings nominate NMD-regulatory variation as a potential modifier of somatic associations with molecular and clinical outcomes, motivating further validation using normal-sample genotypes, alternative interaction models, and detailed characterization of the somatic alterations underlying these candidate associations.

Talk/Poster Title: Assembly-aware single-cell long-read analysis shows that gene repertoire outweighs transcript selection in shaping the predicted NMD fraction across mouse hippocampal cohorts
Author(s): Abu Humayed Azim Fahmid
Abstract: Brain cell types differ in the fraction of their transcripts predicted to undergo nonsense-mediated decay (NMD), but it is unclear whether these differences arise from the genes they express or the transcript isoforms they select within those genes. We analyzed assembly-aware single-cell long-read data from eight postnatal mouse hippocampal samples and an independent validation cohort of 13 aging hippocampal samples. We decomposed cell-type differences in the predicted NMD fraction into gene-repertoire and within-gene transcript-selection components. In the discovery cohort, the median excitatory-neuron versus microglia difference was 1.458 percentage points, of which 1.402 percentage points came from gene repertoire and 0.126 from transcript selection. The median transcript-selection share was 7.6%, and gene repertoire was the larger component in all eight animals. The validation cohort showed the same pattern, with a median transcript-selection share of 7.9% and gene-repertoire dominance in all 13 animals. Transcript selection became prominent only after restricting the analysis to genes with similar abundance between cell types, where the remaining NMD-fraction differences were small. These results show that cell-type variation in predicted NMD fraction is driven mainly by gene-expression composition, with a smaller within-gene transcript-selection component.
